english: Adventure / venture
latin: ausum, ausī n. · adventūra, adventūrae f.
keywords: Adventure / venture ausum, ausī n. adventūra, adventūrae f. Ancient Latin Medieval Latin Modern semantic extension ausum, ausī n. — a daring attempt, venture, undertaking or enterprise; our preferred word for modern adventure when the emphasis is on something voluntarily and boldly undertaken. adventūra, adventūrae f. — a medieval Latin word connected with what happens, chance, fortune, risk or venture; retained here as a secondary word for modern adventure by later semantic extension, especially through the Romance development of the word. Novum ausum suscipiāmus. — Let’s undertake a new adventure. Hodiē novum ausum quaerāmus. — Let’s seek a new adventure today. Nova adventūra nōs exspectat. — A new adventure awaits us; a modern-style use, not presented as an ancient idiom. The English word adventure ultimately belongs to the adventūra family, but its cheerful modern sense is later than the core medieval Latin meanings. For ordinary family speech, prefer ausum when a classical/ancient word is wanted; use adventūra when the later European word-family itself is useful.

english: Security check / security officer / tray
keywords: fābulae fabulae Theodōrus et pater Security check / security officer / tray scrūtātiō, scrūtātiōnis f. Ancient words Working formation scrūtātiō, scrūtātiōnis f. — security check: the fābula’s descriptive term (locūtiō nostra), from scrūtor, scrūtārī, scrūtātus sum — search thoroughly (L&S). It is not a recorded Neo-Latin airport term. custōs, custōdis m./f. — guard; here a security officer, feminine in Fābula VI. cista, cistae f. — box or chest; applied in the fābula to the tray at the security check. sarcinās excutere — search the bags (literally, shake them out; Fābula I); calceōs exuere — take off one’s shoes; see the existing shoe entry. Hīc sumus nōs: haec est Bulgaria — Here we are: this is Bulgaria (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Vidēsne quam longē absit? — Do you see how far away it is? (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Cracōvia ad septentriōnēs est, Bergomum ad merīdiem, sub Alpibus. — Kraków is to the north, Bergamo to the south, below the Alps. (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

english: In the car: get in / get out / car door / window / steering wheel / headlights / brake / park / car park / traffic light
keywords: car get in get out car door window steering wheel headlights brake brakes slow down tyre tire park parking car park parking lot traffic light red light vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: autoraedam īnscendere — get into the car (Traupman 215; īnscendō, Plaut.); dē autoraedā ēgredī — get out of the car (Traupman 215).
ōstiolum, ōstiolī n. — car door (Traupman 215); classically a small door (Columella; Pliny).
fenestella, fenestellae f. — car window (Traupman 219); classically a small window (Columella).
receptāculum sarcinārum — boot, trunk (Traupman 219); see the car entry.
rota moderātrīx — steering wheel (Traupman 218).
lūmināria, lūminārium n. pl. — headlights (Traupman 216); in Late Latin “lamps” (sing. lūmināre).
rotās sufflāmināre — brake (Traupman 215), from sufflāmen, the drag on a wheel (Juv. 8.148 rotam adstringit sufflāmine); cursum reprimere — slow down (Traupman 218).
canthus, canthī m. — tyre: the iron tyre of a wheel (Quint. 1.5.8); canthus cummeus — rubber tyre (Traupman 218).
autoraedam statuere — park the car (Traupman 217); ārea statīva — car park (Traupman 217).
sēmaphorum, sēmaphorī n. — traffic light (Traupman 219: rubrum, flāvum, viride).
cum dē autoraedā ēgressī essent — when they had got out of the car (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
«Cūr cōnsistimus?» «Quia sēmaphorum rubrum est.» — “Why are we stopping?” “Because the light is red.” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Theodōrus, nōmine nōndum nōtō, manū quasi rotam moderātrīcem versāvit — Theo, who did not know the name yet, turned his hand as if on a steering wheel (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
ōstiolō apertō, avum cōnspicātus in complexum ejus ruit — the door opened, he saw Grandpa and ran into his arms (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
Per fenestellam arborēs tam propinquae praeterībant ut eās paene tangere possēs. — Through the window the trees went by so close you could almost touch them. (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
Olīvās lūmināria autoraedae aliam post aliam ē tenebrīs ēdūcēbant. — The headlights brought the olive trees out of the dark one after another. (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
quotiēns avus ad sēmaphorum rubrum rotās sufflāminābat — every time Grandpa braked at a red light (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
Autoraedā in āreā statīvā statūtā — When they had parked the car in the car park (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).

english: Getting about: baggage trolley / ticket office / lift / ferry / fare / pack / check out
keywords: baggage trolley luggage cart ticket office ticket window lift elevator ferry fare pack packing check out hotel bill aisle vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: chīramaxium, chīramaxiī n. — baggage trolley (Traupman 215: chīramaxium sarcinārum); in Petronius (28.4) a small hand-drawn carriage.
ōstiolum, ōstiolī n. — ticket window, ticket office (Traupman 218: ōstiolum tesserārum).
cellula scānsōria — lift, elevator (Traupman 309), after Vitruvius’s climbing machine, the scānsōrium (10.1.1).
nāvis trājectōria — ferry (Traupman 216).
vectūra, vectūrae f. — the fare, transport (Traupman 216); classical, as in prō vectūrā solvere (Cic. Att. 1.3.2).
sarcinās colligere — pack (Traupman 217); ā dēversōriō discēdere post ratiōnem compōnendam — check out of a hotel after settling the bill (Traupman 215).
ambulātiuncula, ambulātiunculae f. — aisle (Traupman 215); in Cicero a short walk or a small walk (Fam. 2.12; Att. 13.29).
hominēs autem cum chīramaxiīs stantēs exspectant suōsque quaerunt — and people stand waiting with their trolleys, looking for their own (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Tesserīs ad ōstiolum ēmptīs — When they had bought tickets at the ticket window (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
Cum cellulā scānsōriā ūnā ascendissent — When they had gone up together in the lift (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
nāvēs trājectōriae lentē prōgredientēs — ferries slowly making their way (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
Sub ipsīs moenibus, vectūrā solūtā, ē raedā dēscendērunt — Right under the walls they paid the fare and got out of the taxi (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Avus et avia, quī in cubiculō proximō dormīverant, sarcinīs collēctīs parātī in vestibulō exspectābant. Ratiōne compositā ā dēversōriō discessum est. — Grandpa and Grandma, who had slept in the next room, had packed and were waiting ready in the lobby. The bill was settled and they checked out. (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
quam pater et fīlius, per ambulātiunculam prōgressī, ūnā intrāvērunt — which father and son went into together, after walking down the aisle (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

english: Dad’s bag: leather bag / wallet / notepad / pen / headphones
keywords: bag leather bag wallet purse notepad notebook pen ballpoint headphones earphones vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: pēra scortea — leather bag (Traupman 117); scorteus “of leather” (Varro, LL 7.84).
crumēna, crumēnae f. — purse, wallet (Traupman 367); classically a small money bag (Plaut.; Hor. Ep. 1.4.11).
pugillārēs, pugillārium m. pl. — notepad (Traupman 30); classically writing tablets (Sen. Ep. 108.6; Pliny).
stilus, stilī m. — pen; Traupman 28 has stilus sphaerātus, a ballpoint. Classically the writing stylus.
auscultābula, auscultābulōrum n. pl. — headphones: our formation (locūtiō nostra), after Traupman’s auscultābulum (p. 124), from auscultāre “listen”.

et duae pērae, altera Theodōrī, altera patris, scortea, in quā ille tēlephōnum, crumēnam, pugillārēs, stilum, auscultābula semper servat — and two bags, one Theo’s, the other Dad’s, made of leather, in which he always keeps his phone, wallet, notepad, pen and headphones (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
